title: Transferring data between threads with message passing
summary: Channels with mpsc, send and recv, ownership transfer through a channel, receiving with a for loop, multiple producers by cloning the sender, sync_channel and backpressure, and pipelines.

sections: TRPL 16.2 Using Message Passing to Transfer Data Between Threads

PR ch19 Channel Features and Performance

blocks.md:
A popular way to make threads cooperate is **message passing**: threads send each other data instead of sharing memory. The Go documentation's slogan sums it up: "Do not communicate by sharing memory; instead, share memory by communicating."

Rust's standard library provides **channels**. A channel has two halves: a **transmitter** (`Sender`) and a **receiver** (`Receiver`). One part of your code sends values into the transmitter; another takes them out of the receiver, in the order they were sent, like rubber ducks floating down a stream.

blocks.explain: `mpsc` means **multiple producer, single consumer**: many senders, one receiver. `send` returns `Err` if the receiver is gone. `recv` **blocks** until a value arrives, and returns `Err` when every sender has been dropped and nothing more can come. `try_recv` returns immediately instead, for a thread with other work to do.

blocks.title: Sending moves ownership
blocks.md:
`send` takes ownership of the value. After sending, the spawned thread can no longer use it, which rules out a whole class of bugs: the receiving thread could be modifying or dropping it.

```rust
tx.send(val).unwrap();
println!("val is {val}"); // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `val`
```

blocks.title: Receiving as an iterator
blocks.md: The receiver can be used as an **iterator**: a `for` loop waits for each value and ends when the channel is closed, which happens when all senders are dropped.

blocks.title: Bounded channels and backpressure
blocks.md: `mpsc::channel()` is **unbounded**: a fast producer can fill memory if the consumer is slow. `mpsc::sync_channel(n)` holds at most `n` messages; `send` blocks when it is full. *Programming Rust* calls this **backpressure**: the slow stage of a pipeline automatically slows the fast one. `sync_channel(0)` is a rendezvous: each send waits for a matching receive.

steps.title: Stages connected by channels
steps.md: *Programming Rust* builds a search index in stages: read files → split into words → build per-file indexes → merge. Each stage is a thread that receives from the previous channel and sends to the next.

steps.title: Each stage is a loop over its receiver
steps.md: A stage owns its receiver and the next sender. When the upstream sender closes, `for x in rx` ends, the stage drops its own sender, and the close propagates down the pipeline.

steps.title: All stages run at once
steps.md: While the reader loads file 3, the tokenizer works on file 2 and the indexer on file 1. On a multi-core machine the throughput is set by the slowest stage.

blocks.title: A two-stage pipeline
blocks.md: Stage 1 sends the numbers 1 to 10. Build stage 2: a thread that receives from the first channel, keeps only even numbers, squares them, and sends them on. `main` sums what comes out.
hints: `thread::spawn(move || { for n in rx1 { if n % 2 == 0 { tx2.send(n * n).unwrap(); } } });`
The starter drops `tx2` right away so it does not hang. If you remove those lines without moving `tx2` into a thread, `rx2.iter()` waits forever, because a sender is still alive.

blocks.title: A worker pool with channels
blocks.goal: Fan work out to several threads and collect results through a channel, preserving order.
blocks.behavior:
- `pub fn fan_out(jobs: Vec<u64>, workers: usize, f: fn(u64) -> u64) -> Vec<u64>`: start `workers` threads (at least 1). Distribute the jobs round-robin (job `i` goes to worker `i % workers`), each worker sends `(index, f(job))` for its jobs into one shared result channel. Return the results **in job order**.
- `pub fn first_match(candidates: Vec<u64>, test: fn(u64) -> bool) -> Option<u64>`: test every candidate on its own thread, each sending the candidate if it passes; return the **smallest** passing candidate, or `None`.
hints: Split the jobs: `let mut buckets: Vec<Vec<(usize, u64)>> = vec![Vec::new(); w];` and push `(i, job)` into `buckets[i % w]`.
For each bucket: `let tx = tx.clone(); thread::spawn(move || for (i, job) in bucket { tx.send((i, f(job))).unwrap(); });`
`drop(tx)` before reading, collect `(i, v)` pairs, sort by `i`, keep the values.
blocks.solution_explain: Sending the index with each result lets the collector restore the original order, whatever order the workers finish in. Both functions drop the original `tx` so the receiver's iterator ends once every worker is done.

questions.q: What happens to a value after `tx.send(val)`?
options: Its ownership moves into the channel; the sender cannot use it
questions.explanation: No shared access, no data race.

questions.q: When does `for msg in rx` stop?
options: When every Sender has been dropped and the channel is empty
questions.explanation: That is why you drop the original tx.

questions.q: What does `sync_channel(2)` do when it already holds 2 messages and a thread calls send?

questions.explanation: It returns Err(Empty) when nothing is waiting.
